overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Husserl's critique of psychologism and his account of givenness. You'll be asked about the definition of psychologism, Husserl's arguments against it, the distinction between act and content, fulfillment, and the principle of all principles.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

options.html: The view that psychology should be studied only through experiments
options.text: The view that psychology should be studied only through experiments
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's a claim about psychological method. Psychologism is the view that logical laws, or the contents of thought, are grounded in facts about human psychology.

options.html: The view that logical laws are grounded in facts about human psychology
options.text: The view that logical laws are grounded in facts about human psychology
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Psychologism grounds logic, and the contents of thought more generally, in facts about how human minds work. It makes logic a branch of psychology.

options.html: The view that the mind can't be studied scientifically at all
options.text: The view that the mind can't be studied scientifically at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Psychologism assumes the mind can be studied scientifically. It's the view that logical laws, or the contents of thought, are grounded in facts about human psychology.

options.html: The view that logic has no connection to how people reason
options.text: The view that logic has no connection to how people reason
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's closer to the opposite of psychologism. Psychologism is the view that logical laws, or the contents of thought, are grounded in facts about human psychology.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are arguments Husserl gives against psychologism? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Logical laws are exact, while psychological laws are vague
options.text: Logical laws are exact, while psychological laws are vague
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Psychological laws hold roughly and with exceptions. Logical laws are exact, so they can't be psychological laws.

options.html: Logical laws are known a priori, not by induction
options.text: Logical laws are known a priori, not by induction
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Psychological laws are learned by observation and induction. Logical laws are known independently of observation.

options.html: Psychologism leads to a self-undermining relativism
options.text: Psychologism leads to a self-undermining relativism
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! If logic depended on the human constitution, truth would be relative to the species. That view relies on the very notion of truth it denies.

options.html: Psychology isn't a genuine empirical science
options.text: Psychology isn't a genuine empirical science
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl didn't deny that psychology is a science. His target was the claim that logic is grounded in psychology.

options.html: Human beings can never think logically at all
options.text: Human beings can never think logically at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl made no such claim. His arguments concern the grounding of logical laws, not whether people reason well.

forms.stemHtml: You and a colleague both judge that the meeting starts at noon. How would Husserl describe this situation?

options.html: One act of judging, with two different contents
options.text: One act of judging, with two different contents
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. There are two acts, one in each of you, but they share one ideal content: that the meeting starts at noon.

options.html: Two acts of judging, with one shared ideal content
options.text: Two acts of judging, with one shared ideal content
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Each judging is a real act, a mental event in one person at one time. What is judged is one ideal content, the same for both of you.

options.html: Two acts of judging, with two private contents
options.text: Two acts of judging, with two private contents
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl's point is that the content isn't private. There are two acts, but they share one ideal content.

options.html: One act of judging, shared between two minds
options.text: One act of judging, shared between two minds
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Acts are events in particular people, so there are two acts. What they share is one ideal content.

forms.stemHtml: When you think of a friend's absent face, your act is an intention. When the friend walks in and you see the face you meant, the intention is .

options.html: empty
options.text: empty
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! An empty intention means its object without the object being given in intuition.

options.html: originary
options.text: originary
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Originary intuition gives its object in person, and the absent face isn't given. Thinking of it is an empty intention.

options.html: ideal
options.text: ideal
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. "Ideal" describes contents, not kinds of intention. Thinking of an absent face is an empty intention.

options.html: disappointed
options.text: disappointed
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. An intention is disappointed when what's given doesn't match what was meant. Here it matches, so the intention is fulfilled.

options.html: fulfilled
options.text: fulfilled
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Fulfillment is the experienced coincidence of what was meant with what is given.

options.html: psychologized
options.text: psychologized
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That isn't a term in Husserl's account. When the face you meant is given, the intention is fulfilled.

forms.stemHtml: What does the limit clause of the principle of all principles add?

options.html: It says that only scientific theories can limit intuition
options.text: It says that only scientific theories can limit intuition
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The principle holds that no theory can override what is given. The limit clause says that what is given is to be accepted only within the limits in which it is given.

options.html: It says that introspective reports can never be mistaken
options.text: It says that introspective reports can never be mistaken
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The limit clause does the opposite. It restricts authority to what is actually given, which is often partial and can be corrected.

options.html: It restricts what is given to the limits in which it is given
options.text: It restricts what is given to the limits in which it is given
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! What is given is to be accepted only within the limits of its givenness. A house seen from the front licenses claims about the front, not the back.

options.html: It says that intuition gives objects only through images
options.text: It says that intuition gives objects only through images
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Originary intuition gives its object in person, not through images. The limit clause restricts what is given to the limits in which it is given.

title: Against Psychologism
